entries.title: Amharic at a glance
body: Amharic is the working language of Ethiopia's federal government, spoken by about 35 million people as a first language and by many more as a second. It is a Semitic language, related to Tigrinya, Arabic and Hebrew, and is the second most spoken Semitic language after Arabic.
The verb comes last. Nouns and verbs take endings and prefixes for person, number and gender, and “you” has separate forms for a man, a woman, and a respected person.

entries.title: How the fidel works
body: Amharic is written in the Ethiopic script, called ፊደል (fidel). Each character is a consonant plus a vowel. A base shape has seven forms, the “orders”, made by adding small strokes, rings or bends for each vowel.
The script comes from Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia, which is still used in the Orthodox church. Words are separated by spaces today; older texts use ፡, and ። ends a sentence.

entries.title: “To be”
entries.body: ነው and its forms come at the end of the sentence and agree with the subject.

entries.title: Numbers and Ethiopic numerals
entries.body: Ethiopic numerals have no zero and have separate signs for tens and for 100. Today they are used mostly for dates and in formal writing; prices use the digits 0–9.

examples.e: How are you? (to a man / to a woman)

entries.title: The coffee ceremony
body: The coffee ceremony (ቡና ማፍላት, buna maflat) is a central part of Ethiopian hospitality. Green beans are roasted in a pan in front of the guests, ground by hand, and brewed in a clay pot called a ጀበና (jebena), while incense burns.
Coffee is served in small cups in three rounds, called abol, tona and bereka. Staying for all three is polite.
